title: A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) for Intent→Configuration NetOps: Null Results on a Synthetic Verifier-Checked Task Bank
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired experiment that evaluated whether a deterministic verifier plus a bounded LLM-guided repair loop (Generate–Verify–Repair, GVR) reduces verifier-detected semantic invariant violations for intent→device-configuration translation. The confirmatory design used a public synthetic NetOps task bank (N = 240 paired tasks), gpt-5-mini as the generator, and a pybatfish-style deterministic validator. Execution used shared-initial-candidate semantics (one generated candidate per task reused across arms) and allowed at most one bounded repair attempt per task. All planned episodes completed (planned_episode_count = 480; completed_episode_count = 480) with model_calls_used = 240 (shared-generation). Every generated candidate satisfied the deterministic verifier in both arms: n11 = 240, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0. The paired estimate (rate_GVR − rate_baseline) = 0.0; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00; paired-bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Two preregistration/execution issues constrain inference: (1) shared-generation semantics invalidated the preregistered power calculation that assumed independent per-condition generation, and (2) a prespecified schema-constrained baseline comparison (GVR vs B) was not executed and no recorded rationale appears in the archive. Conservatively interpreted, bounded GVR provided no verifier-detectable benefit in this artifact-backed setting because no verifier-detectable errors were produced; results do not generalize beyond the executed semantics, model, task bank, or verifier. We release and analyze authoritative archived artifacts and recommend reproducible follow-ups (independent per-condition generation, adversarial injections, multi-model runs, and broader verifier coverage).

sections.introduction:
Automated translation from operator intent to concrete device configuration holds promise for accelerating NetOps, but it raises safety and correctness concerns: stochastic LLMs can output syntactically plausible yet semantically incorrect commands that violate network invariants (reachability, workflow ordering, ACLs). To mitigate these risks, practical pipelines interpose deterministic validators and iterative repair loops (generate–verify–repair, GVR) that detect and correct mechanically checkable defects before execution. Empirical and systems literature supports the plausibility of this architecture for reducing syntactic and some semantic failures, but open questions remain about measurable operational benefit when generator performance, verifier coverage, evaluation semantics, or experimental design choices limit detectable discordance.

This work answers a narrowly scoped, preregistered research question with an artifact-backed paired experiment: given a frozen task bank, a single generator/prompt pairing (gpt-5-mini), a pybatfish-style deterministic verifier, and bounded-repair GVR semantics, does inserting the verifier plus a single bounded LLM-guided repair reduce verifier-detected invariant violations relative to (A) unconstrained LLM generation and (B) schema-constrained decoding? We preregistered estimands, power assumptions, and analysis, executed the run under archived adapter settings, and report authoritative counts and statistics from the archived analysis executor. The archive shows a degenerate null outcome: every shared-generated candidate satisfied the verifier in both arms, producing zero discordant pairs (n11 = 240; n10 = n01 = n00 = 0). We explain why the design and execution semantics produced this outcome, document the procedural deviation (the prespecified constrained-baseline comparison was not executed), and provide operational recommendations and reproducible next steps to restore sensitivity and measure GVR’s value under conditions that enable discordance.
sections.related_work:
We position this study against three intersecting literatures.

LLM reliability and hallucinations. Surveys and empirical work show that LLMs commonly hallucinate or fabricate code and structured artifacts across domains, motivating verifier-in-the-loop architectures (e.g., studies of hallucination detection and generate-and-validate repair). These works motivate generate–verify styles but also caution that improvements often focus on mechanically checkable properties rather than full domain semantics.

GVR, constrained decoding, and verifier-assisted pipelines. Prior systems work reports that grammar- or schema-constrained decoding and generate–verify–repair pipelines raise syntactic and executable success rates and reduce surface-level hallucinations. Case reports indicate improved compilation or grammar-valid outputs, but semantic correctness for domain-specific invariants (e.g., NetOps workflow ordering or cross-device policies) remains less comprehensively measured.

NetOps verification and intent-translation. The NetOps literature advocates rigorous verifier-driven evaluation (reachability, ACL/policy invariants) and human-in-the-loop governance for high-stakes changes. Recent intent→configuration prototypes and benchmarks have started integrating deterministic validators, but standardization of semantics and evaluation protocols is still emerging.

Nearest-work comparison matrix (compact). We compare the present run to the closest verified studies (entries use verified bibliographic records):
- NetConfEval (2024): benchmarked LLMs on configuration tasks; focused on per-output accuracy and syntax; differs by being a benchmark rather than a preregistered paired GVR confirmatory test.
- MeshAgent (Zhou et al., 2025): prototype for LLM-enabled network management with verifier components; differs by exploratory system design and not following a preregistered paired inferential protocol.
- GRAMMAR-LLM / grammar-constrained decoding (Findings ACL 2025): demonstrates constrained decoding benefits for syntax; differs because syntactic gains do not automatically imply semantic invariant improvements measured by a NetOps verifier.
- ConU (Conformal uncertainty in LLMs, Findings EMNLP 2024): focuses on uncertainty calibration; differs in estimands and domain (general correctness coverage guarantees vs. targeted GVR efficacy in NetOps).

This study differs by (a) preregistering a paired confirmatory estimand for verifier-detectable semantic violations, (b) freezing the analysis executor, (c) archiving execution artifacts, and (d) explicitly testing a bounded GVR intervention under tightly specified generation semantics (shared-initial-candidate) and repair budget.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary estimand. The study was preregistered (study_id c1_gvr_semantic_eval_prereg_v1). The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline: the within-pair difference in verifier-detected semantic-violation rates between the GVR (guarded) arm and a baseline arm. The preregistration specified two prespecified primary comparisons: (C vs A) GVR vs unconstrained generation and (C vs B) GVR vs schema-constrained decoding; Bonferroni correction across the two comparisons was planned. The frozen analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1) and analysis plan (exact paired McNemar-style test, paired bootstrap CIs) were archived prior to data observation.

Design, task bank, and verifier. Confirmatory sample: N = 240 tasks formed by 12 topology/policy clusters × 20 tasks per cluster (public synthetic NetOps task bank). Each task encodes initial device state, intent text, workflow constraints, and an expected final state. The deterministic validator implements pybatfish-style semantic predicates and produces structured diagnostics (violation_count, violations list, parsed_command_count, required_command_count). Scoring rule: full_intent_constraint_validation using deterministic_netops_validator_v5.

Adapter and model configuration. The adapter_family used was hosted_netops_gvr_v1. The requested generator was gpt-5-mini. Execution-mode semantics crucial to interpretation: the preregistration allowed either independent per-condition generation or shared-initial-candidate semantics; the archived adapter configuration executed shared_initial_candidate generation_semantics (one initial generation per task reused across arms) and permitted at most one bounded repair attempt per task (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). Model-call budget was set to 480 but under shared-generation the run used model_calls_used = 240 (one shared call per task).

Planned statistical power. The preregistered power plan (independent-generation assumption) targeted an absolute paired reduction of 10 percentage points with N = 240. That power calculation assumed independent stochastic variation between arms; as executed, shared-generation semantics removed the independent stochasticity and therefore invalidated the preregistered power assumptions for the realized run.

Execution controls and missingness. The preregistration included explicit exclusion rules and a missingness plan ('complete_pair_primary'); technical restarts were permitted only for infrastructure recovery and to be logged. The archived execution manifest reports planned_episode_count = 480, completed_episode_count = 480, failed_episode_count = 0, and model_calls_used = 240. Analysis and reconciliation artifacts (condition summaries, paired contingency tables, deterministic reconciliation) are archived as the authoritative record.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and observed outcomes (artifact-backed). The archived execution and reconciliation artifacts show planned_episode_count = 480, completed_episode_count = 480, failed_episode_count = 0, complete_pair_count = 240, and model_calls_used = 240 under shared-initial-candidate semantics. For every task the archived shared initial candidate matched both arm responses and satisfied the verifier predicates; repair_applied = false for all episodes.

Primary confirmatory statistics (archival numbers): contingency counts: n11 = 240 (both arms accepted), n10 = 0 (guarded only), n01 = 0 (baseline only), n00 = 0 (both rejected). Observed rates: baseline_success_rate = 1.0; guarded_success_rate = 1.0; paired estimate (rate_GVR − rate_baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00. Paired-bootstrap 95% CI (paired_bootstrap_percentile; 10,000 resamples; seed 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Analysis artifacts (paired_contingency_table.csv, condition_summary.csv, analysis_log.jsonl) are archived and authoritative for these quantities.

Degeneracy and cause. The zero-discordance outcome makes the paired McNemar test degenerate: with no within-pair disagreements there is no information to estimate a differential effect. Two artifact-supported mechanisms explain this degeneracy: (1) task/verifier alignment — for the synthetic task bank, the chosen prompt+model pairing consistently produced verifier-acceptable candidates; and (2) shared-generation semantics — reusing a single generated candidate across arms removes per-arm stochasticity and therefore removes the within-pair variation GVR could exploit.

Prespecified but unexecuted comparison. The preregistration listed two primary comparisons (C vs A and C vs B). The archived execution artifacts document only the adapter-configured paired experiment comparing unconstrained baseline (A) to guarded GVR (C) under shared_initial_candidate semantics. The prespecified schema-constrained-baseline comparison (C vs B) was not executed; the execution artifacts contain no recorded rationale for this omission. We therefore treat this omission as an unresolved procedural deviation and report it explicitly.

Representative examples and cluster summaries. Representative per-task validator traces archived in execution/scoring/ show validation_before and validation_after blocks with violation_count = 0 for all illustrated tasks. Cluster-stratified acceptance summaries in the archived task manifest and analysis artifacts show 100% acceptance in both arms across all 12 clusters for this synthetic bank under the executed semantics.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and limits. Conservatively interpreted, the artifact-backed null indicates that bounded GVR (one allowed repair) did not add verifier-detectable value in this specific execution because there were no verifier-detectable errors to correct. This does not imply that GVR lacks value generally: measurable benefit requires (a) generator failure modes that produce verifier-detectable errors, (b) evaluation semantics that preserve per-arm stochastic variation (independent generation), and (c) verifier coverage sufficient to reveal operationally relevant violations.

Design lessons and operational recommendations (artifact-grounded):
1) Restore independent per-condition generation. Re-executing with independent_condition_generation = true (the preregistered alternative) would restore discordance potential; the same task manifest and RNG seeds are archived to support deterministic reruns. 2) Inject adversarial or golden-reference tasks. The preregistration planned 10% golden tasks to validate verifier sensitivity; including such tasks can validate oracle soundness and avoid overfitting to a permissive verifier. 3) Expand model and prompt scope. Multi-model runs measure cross-model generality and expose generator-dependent failure modes. 4) Increase repair budget and track repair-iteration distributions to measure repair efficacy beyond a single bounded attempt. 5) Broaden verifier predicates or integrate stronger formal checks to reduce oracle incompleteness; prior-method gaps indicate opportunities for SMT or synthesis hybrids.

Threats to validity. Internal validity is reduced because the executed shared-generation semantics contradict the independent-generation assumption used for the preregistered power calculation. Construct validity is limited by verifier completeness: passing deterministic_netops_validator_v5 does not guarantee absence of all operational risks beyond the encoded invariants. External validity is constrained by the synthetic task bank, single model (gpt-5-mini), single repair budget, and single verifier. Conclusion validity is limited because the zero-discordant outcome provides no evidence for GVR efficacy under the executed semantics.

Relation to prior work. Our artifact-backed null aligns with the broader literature’s caution that measurable benefits of verifier-involved architectures depend on evaluation semantics and oracle coverage: constrained decoding and GVR reduce syntactic and some mechanical failures, but demonstrating semantic improvements requires tasks and verifiers that surface such errors under realistic generator variation.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment assessing whether a bounded generate–verify–repair intervention reduces verifier-detected semantic violations on a synthetic intent→configuration NetOps task bank. Under the executed shared-initial-candidate semantics and the chosen generator/prompt pairing, every shared-generated candidate satisfied the deterministic verifier in both arms (n11 = 240), producing a degenerate null (paired estimate = 0.0; exact McNemar p = 1.00; paired-bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]). Two procedural issues constrain generalization: the executed shared-generation semantics invalidated the preregistered independent-generation power assumptions, and a prespecified constrained-baseline comparison (C vs B) was not executed. We therefore conclude only that bounded GVR provided no additional verifier-detectable benefit in this specific, artifact-grounded setting. We publish the authoritative archived artifacts so others can reproduce the accounting and extend evaluation under independent-generation, adversarial, multi-model, and expanded-verifier regimes to more robustly assess GVR’s operational value.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and verifier scope: N = 240 tasks were synthetic and evaluated against a pybatfish-style deterministic validator; results may not generalize to production topologies, vendor-specific syntax, or semantic invariants not encoded in the verifier.

Shared-generation semantics: the archived run used generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (one initial generation per task reused across arms). This design reduced model-call cost but also removed per-arm stochastic variation and therefore reduced sensitivity to detect GVR benefits that rely on independent per-condition generator variability; the preregistered power calculation assumed independent per-condition generation and therefore does not apply to the executed design.
Single-model evaluation: the experiment used one generator (gpt-5-mini); cross-model generality is not established.
Repair budget: only a single bounded repair iteration was permitted; different or larger repair budgets or iterative strategies might produce different outcomes.
Verifier completeness risk: passing the deterministic verifier does not guarantee absence of all operational risks (unobserved invariants or properties outside the verifier model).

Prespecified comparison not executed: the preregistration included a prespecified schema-constrained-baseline comparison (C vs B) that was not executed in the archived run; the artifacts do not record a rationale, which is an unresolved procedural limitation.
